title: Saying “the” with Norwegian Noun Endings
goal: Use Norwegian definite noun endings for simple singular nouns and basic plural nouns.

objectives.statement: Use Norwegian definite noun endings for simple singular nouns and basic plural nouns.

spans.value: After a community cooking class, Nora and Amir are collecting their things. Several bags, cups, and books are still on a table near the door.
Er dette koppen din?
Nei, koppen min er blå.
Hva med boka?
Boka er di. Du la den på bordet.

blocks.translation: The book is yours. You put it on the table.

spans.value: Ja, selvfølgelig. Men hvor er posen min?

blocks.translation: Yes, of course. But where is my bag?

spans.value: Er posen under stolene?

blocks.translation: Is the bag under the chairs?

spans.value: Nei. Vent — der er den, mellom koppene!

blocks.translation: No. Wait—there it is, between the cups!

spans.value: Bra. Nå har vi boka, koppen og posen.

blocks.translation: Good. Now we have the book, the cup, and the bag.

spans.value: The first time an object is mentioned, Norwegian can introduce it with en, ei, or et:
Once Nora and Amir know which object they mean, they use forms such as koppen, boka, and posen. Norwegian normally expresses simple English the by adding an ending to the noun.
A noun used for an unspecified or newly introduced thing is in the indefinite form (ubestemt form). A noun used for a particular, identifiable thing is in the definite form (bestemt form).
Compare:
Indefinite / Definite

en.value: The book is on the table.
The map is in the car.

spans.value: English places the before a noun. In these simple Norwegian noun phrases, definiteness belongs at the end of the noun:
These endings connect with noun gender, which you already know from en, ei, and et.
Masculine nouns
For a simple masculine singular noun, add -en:
The ending is attached directly to the noun. There is no separate word corresponding to English the.

no.value: Jeg finner en nøkkel. Nøkkelen ligger ved døra.

en.value: I find a key. The key is by the door.

spans.value: The first sentence introduces a key. The second sentence refers to that same key.
Feminine nouns
When a feminine noun is introduced with ei, its definite singular form commonly ends in -a:

no.value: Det står ei jente utenfor. Jenta venter på bussen.

en.value: There is a girl outside. The girl is waiting for the bus.

spans.value: Bokmål also permits masculine forms for many feminine nouns, such as en bok → boken. This chapter uses the clear feminine pattern ei bok → boka consistently. Both systems are Bokmål, but do not mix the introduction and ending accidentally while learning the pattern.
Neuter nouns
For a simple neuter singular noun, add -et:
Sometimes the spelling looks slightly different because the noun already ends in -e:
Learn the complete definite form as part of the noun pattern.

no.value: Hun åpner et vindu. Vinduet er stort.

en.value: She opens a window. The window is large.

spans.value: Use the noun’s gender to select its basic definite singular ending:
Gender / Indefinite singular / Definite singular
A compact rule:

statement.value: For simple singular nouns, remove en, ei, or et from before the noun and attach the corresponding definite ending: usually -en, -a, or -et.

spans.value: This is a form rule, but context still determines whether the noun should be definite.
Compare these small exchanges:

en.value: Yes, but the pen is empty.
The handbag is by the door.

spans.value: The speaker first asks about any suitable pen. The reply then describes the particular pen that has been identified.
The first sentence introduces the bakery. The second treats it as known information.
Again, the movement is from a newly introduced object to a particular known object.
Common mistake: adding a separate “the”
Do not translate English structure word for word:
not a separate word plus stol
For a simple noun with no adjective, the ending itself carries the meaning of the.
Another common mistake is leaving en, ei, or et in front while also adding the definite ending. In this lesson’s simple noun phrases, use either the indefinite form or the definite form:
Do not combine both patterns.

sections.title: More than one: definite plural nouns

spans.value: Norwegian also adds an ending when a plural noun means the books, the chairs, or the apples.
Start by comparing indefinite and definite plural forms:
Indefinite plural / Definite plural
For these common plural patterns, the definite plural ends in -ene. When the indefinite plural ends in -er, the change often looks like this:
The final -r disappears before -ene.
Some nouns have a changed plural stem, but the definite ending still attaches to the plural form:
The vowel change in bok → bøker belongs to the noun’s plural pattern. The definite form needed here is bøkene.
Neuter nouns ending in -e often follow the same visible pattern:
A few very common neuter plurals have no ending in the indefinite plural and use -a in the definite plural:
Treat barna as a common complete form. For the regular nouns used throughout most of this chapter, -ene is the central definite plural pattern.
The plural meaning follows the same basic logic as the singular meaning.

no.value: Det står stoler i rommet. Stolene er nye.

en.value: There are chairs in the room. The chairs are new.

no.value: Nora finner bøker på bordet. Bøkene tilhører læreren.

en.value: Nora finds books on the table. The books belong to the teacher.

no.value: Vi kjøper epler. Eplene er til kurset.

en.value: We buy apples. The apples are for the class.

spans.value: In the original scene, Amir asks:
Er posen under stolene?

blocks.translation: Is the bag under the chairs?

spans.value: He does not mean any chairs anywhere. He means the visible chairs near the lost-property table. Later, Nora sees her bag:
Der er den, mellom koppene!

blocks.translation: There it is, between the cups!

spans.value: Again, koppene means a particular group of cups in their shared surroundings.
A few minutes later, the class teacher comes back.
Har dere funnet tingene deres?
Ja. Veska og boka er mine.

blocks.translation: Yes. The handbag and the book are mine.

spans.value: Og koppen er min.
Flott. Kan dere sette stolene ved bordet?

blocks.translation: Great. Can you put the chairs by the table?

spans.value: Ja. Skal koppene stå på kjøkkenet?

blocks.translation: Yes. Should the cups be in the kitchen?

spans.value: Ja, og posene kan stå ved døra.

blocks.translation: Yes, and the bags can be by the door.

spans.value: The scene now contains both definite singular and definite plural nouns:
Each noun identifies one known object or a known group. Norwegian does this through endings rather than a separate simple equivalent of English the.

prompt.value: Choose the explanation that fits the dialogue.

options.text: The objects are identifiable, but en, ei or et must still stand before each noun.
options.why: In these simple noun phrases, the definite ending replaces the indefinite article.

options.text: Koppen, boka and posen identify particular objects that Nora and Amir can distinguish in the situation.
options.why: The dialogue treats each noun as an identifiable object, so Norwegian marks definiteness with a noun ending.

options.text: The three nouns introduce objects that Nora and Amir have not identified.
options.why: This reading confuses a later reference to an identifiable object with the first mention of an unspecified object.

prompt.value: Choose the sentence pair that shows a transition from something new to something familiar.

options.text: I gangen henger jakka. Ei jakke er våt.
options.why: This presents the jacket as known before introducing it as an unspecified object.

options.text: I gangen henger ei jakke. Ei jakke er våt.

options.why: The first sentence introduces a jacket, and the second identifies that same jacket with the definite form.

prompt.value: At the picnic table in the park there is one basket, one book (ei bok), one apple, several cups, and several bags. Write a message to a friend and say where each thing or group is so your friend can get them. Use the definite form of each noun.

payload.judge_prompt: Check gating criteria picnic-items, audience-purpose, definite-forms and comprehensibility. Record singular-ending-observation and plural-ending-observation diagnostically; criterion ids ending in -observation never cause failure.

criteria.instruction: States a location for the basket, book, apple, cups and bags.
Functions as a message to a friend who needs to collect the listed things.
Uses the definite form of each established noun, not the indefinite form.
Uses standard Norwegian vocabulary and word order so a Norwegian reader can understand and act on every location; a message that is not standard Norwegian fails this criterion.
Observation only: note which definite singular endings appear for the basket, book and apple; never fail on this observation.
Observation only: note which definite plural endings appear for the cups and bags; never fail on this observation.
